sections.title: KRFC AM 1313 Internet Talk Radio
sections.content:
This is an April 1st joke document. The memo presents itself as a program guide for KRFC AM 1313 Internet Talk Radio, a fictional radio station broadcast over the Internet serving the San Francisco Bay Area and available via FTP and the vat audio tool.

The RFC is written in the voice of a radio announcer and lists a fictional programming schedule for Wednesday, April 1, 1992, complete with guest appearances by real networking researchers and engineers.
sections.eli5: This is a joke pretending there is an Internet radio station with funny shows about networking.

sections.title: Sample Programming Highlights
sections.content:
The schedule features shows with names like Hacker's Hour, Nighttime News, Late At Night With Ole, and The Protocol Police. Each description humorously touches on real Internet topics: David Mills and the Doppler effect, OSPF routing protocol testing, ATM networks, NFS implementations, and DES encryption.

Other shows include Lunch with Lynch (with Vint Cerf substituting for the vacationing Dan Lynch) and Two by Four Time (where Marshall Rose "takes out his two-by-four" to correct protocol violations at IETF meetings). The final show, Securely Speaking, jokingly offers listeners a chance to win money and a trip to Ft. Meade for decrypting a DES message.
sections.eli5: Fake shows make jokes about real Internet things, like routing protocols, encryption, and what engineers argue about.

sections.title: The Humor and the Community
sections.content:
The memo gently satirizes IETF meetings, Internet personalities, and common networking debates (such as whether ATM is "Another Technical Mistake"). It references real people in networking roles and real protocols, but presents them in absurd situations: debugging TCP/IP from a hot tub, security experts reading encrypted messages on the radio, and discussions about children learning networking.

The RFC demonstrates the playfulness and self-awareness of the Internet engineering community, showing that even while managing critical infrastructure, engineers could laugh at themselves and their work.
sections.eli5: It is a friendly joke that makes fun of networking experts and their arguments, written by people who actually work with those experts.
